artworks.title: Bellerophon and the Chimera (Attic red-figure epinetron)
artworks.description: The edge of an Attic red-figure epinetron — a curved ceramic guard a woman wore over her thigh while preparing wool for weaving — painted with the Corinthian hero Bellerophon mounted on the winged horse Pegasus as he drives his spear into the fire-breathing Chimera, the lion-goat-serpent monster of Lycia. Made in Athens around 425–420 BC and now in the National Archaeological Museum of Athens (inv. 2179), it is one of the finest classical renderings of the hero's defining exploit and shows how the Pegasus-and-Chimera image had become a fixed visual emblem even on everyday domestic objects.

artworks.title: Plate with Bellerophon on Pegasus slaying the Chimera (Apulian red-figure)
artworks.description: An Apulian red-figure plate attributed to the Baltimore Painter, a leading South Italian vase-painter of the late 4th century BC, showing Bellerophon seated on a galloping Pegasus and thrusting downward at the Chimera that rears beneath the horse. Held in the deposits of the Museo Nazionale Romano (Palazzo Massimo, Rome), it documents the spread of the Bellerophon myth into the Greek colonies of southern Italy and the ornate, theatrical style those workshops brought to heroic combat scenes.

artworks.title: Bellerophon Killing the Chimera (Hellenistic pebble mosaic)
artworks.description: A Hellenistic Greek pebble mosaic from Rhodes depicting Bellerophon astride Pegasus as he spears the Chimera below. Dating to roughly 300–270 BC and now in the Archaeological Museum of Rhodes, it is an early example of the floor-mosaic tradition that would carry the hero's image across the ancient Mediterranean; the rhythmic black-and-white pebble technique freezes the airborne attack at the instant of the kill.

artworks.title: Bellerophon Riding Pegasus and Killing the Chimera (Gallo-Roman mosaic)
artworks.description: The central medallion of a vast Gallo-Roman floor mosaic — about 110 square metres in total — showing Bellerophon on Pegasus plunging his lance into the Chimera, framed by acanthus borders and swan motifs. Discovered at Autun in 1830 and today displayed in the Musée Rolin, it shows how thoroughly the Greek hero was absorbed into Roman provincial art, where Bellerophon's triumph over the monster was read as an allegory of order overcoming chaos and adorned the grandest domestic floors of Roman Gaul.

popCulture.title: Pegasus (constellation)
popCulture.description: The winged horse Bellerophon rode became a northern constellation — the hero's mount fixed in the autumn sky long after the rider fell.

popCulture.title: Bellerophon Taming Pegasus
popCulture.creator: Jacques Lipchitz
popCulture.description: Lipchitz's monumental bronze outside Columbia Law School restages the Corinthian hero mastering Pegasus — myth as a modern emblem of reason bridling inspiration.

popCulture.title: 51 Pegasi b
popCulture.description: The first exoplanet found around a Sun-like star was unofficially dubbed Bellerophon — the Corinthian hero's name carried to a hot Jupiter in the constellation of his winged horse.

music.title: Bellérophon
music.description: Lully's tragédie lyrique for the Paris Opéra restages the Corinthian hero against a summoned Chimera — one of his greatest Baroque successes, the Lycian monster as court spectacle.

music.title: Il Bellerofonte
music.description: Mysliveček's Naples opera seria returns Bellerophon to the Teatro San Carlo — the hero who tamed Pegasus set for Gabrielli and Raaff at the height of opera seria fashion.
